suite_baseline.reconciliation: As recorded in parity/control-plane.ledger.json: 2194 collected + 5 modules skipped at collection time = 2199. Unchanged by this belt.

subsystem.name: secretary
subsystem.note: Gate item 8's rehearsal, interlock tests/secretary, 2 files. One ledger per source file (D-0019). The belt is the behavioural and structural halves of a REHEARSAL (interlock Issue #21, interlock D-0022), not item 8's discharge; interlock Q-0011 is open and no numeric latency threshold is stated or used anywhere in the belt.

file.note: The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order; all 5 pass there (measured 2026-08-29 against the shared read-only clone of interlock at 65f36c5, `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q tests/secretary/ -p no:cacheprovider`: 11 passed, of which 5 are tests/secretary/test_structural.py's).

systematic_mappings.to: `ts.createSourceFile(..., setParentNodes=true)` + a recursive `ts.forEachChild` visitor over each `src/secretary/**/*.ts`
systematic_mappings.why: The source prefers `ast` over a regex because the escapes that matter -- an import in a function body, one behind TYPE_CHECKING -- are exactly what a line-oriented pattern gets wrong. The same is true in TypeScript, plus two more routes a regex or a scan of built JavaScript would miss: `import type` (erased at emit) and dynamic `import()`. `typescript` is already a devDependency and `test/canary/structural.test.ts` sets the precedent in this repository.

systematic_mappings.from: Python relative-import resolution: level 1 is the package importing itself (exempt), level >= 2 escapes to a `claude_org_runtime` sibling (an offence); absolute imports tested against a dotted root allowlist
systematic_mappings.to: `resolve(dirname(importingFile), specifier)` for relative specifiers, then containment in `PACKAGE_DIR`; bare specifiers tested against `ALLOWED_IMPORTS`
systematic_mappings.why: TypeScript has no package-dotted namespace to test a prefix against. Resolving to an absolute path is what stops `../session/index.js` from being judged by its bare tail -- the very slip the source's level rule exists to prevent -- and asks the source's question ('does this leave the package?') without one. Identical to the resolution `test/canary/structural.test.ts` already uses.

Four of the source's five have no Node module to import: `__future__` is a compiler directive, `dataclasses` is `class`/`interface` syntax, `collections.deque` is the `Array` builtin, and `itertools.count` is a `number` field. Only the clock is a module, and `node:process` is where Node keeps the monotonic one. The list is SHORTER, not looser: `node:worker_threads` is absent for exactly the reason `threading` is absent from the source's -- the boundary must have nothing to wait on.

systematic_mappings.from: `PKG_ROOT.rglob("*.py")` -- recursive, so a later `secretary/web/` subpackage is scanned too
systematic_mappings.to: a recursive directory walk, filtered to `*.ts` for scanning, with an explicit (currently empty) `NON_MODULE_FILES` allowlist and any other non-`.ts` file raising
systematic_mappings.why: The recursion is the source's own stated move and is kept for its stated reason. The explicit allowlist is `docs/test-translation-conventions.md` section 10, instance 3: an extension-defined subject set silently stopped covering the fencing package's most security-relevant file the day it shipped as `.mjs`, and stayed green. Naming the exception makes the next added artifact a red test rather than a quiet narrowing.

systematic_mappings.from: `_called_names`: attribute calls by `.attr`, bare calls by `.id`, with `from x import y as z` aliases resolved to the original name
systematic_mappings.to: the same, plus element-access calls (`obj["readFileSync"](...)`) read off the string literal
systematic_mappings.why: The alias resolution is the source's, added at its own review round 4 for the stated reason that without it the ban is a spelling check rather than a property. The element-access route is TypeScript's extra way to write the same call without a dotted name, and is the analogue of the source's alias hole rather than a new assertion; it is probed in the target-only case below.

systematic_mappings.from: `assert not offenders, "message"` over a dict of file -> offending names
systematic_mappings.why: House style, and it keeps the source's reporting shape: the failure names the file AND what it did, rather than only that something failed. Each probe assertion in the target-only case additionally names which escape route it defends, so a regression identifies the route.

systematic_mappings.from: `assert set(secretary_pkg.__all__) == {...}` -- read off the imported module at runtime
systematic_mappings.to: the barrel's named-export list, read off its syntax tree, with a bare `export * from` recorded as an offending pseudo-name
systematic_mappings.why: TypeScript has no `__all__`; the export statement IS the surface. Reading it from the syntax rather than from a loaded module keeps this file's subject uniform (every case here asserts about the tree) and catches the one spelling a runtime read would not distinguish -- `export *`, which hands back the whole module including the status vocabulary and the private item type the barrel deliberately omits.

ids: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > target-only -- the two scans catch the ways around them
target_only_tests.why: The source's structural file has no probe case; `test/canary/structural.test.ts` does, and for the reason that applies here too -- a guard is only as good as what it would have caught, and this port had to REWRITE both scans in a different language. The probe defends the machinery the port wrote (type-only import, a relative specifier climbing out of the package, `require()` in a function body, dynamic `import()` in a function body, an aliased blocking call, an element-access blocking call), not a property of the source, which is what makes it target-only rather than part of case 1 or 3.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: Every case here asserts about the source tree, not about runtime behaviour, so the whole file is able to go green by losing its subject -- a package that was deleted, or one whose modules stopped being scanned, would pass most of these vacuously.
inherited_limitations.why: The source's own limitation, and the source's own three defences are carried: the file set is a directory listing rather than a hand-written list, a non-TypeScript file in the package fails the walk rather than being skipped, and an empty walk raises. The target-only probe closes the fourth gap by proving the scans see what they claim to see.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `BLOCKING_CALL_NAMES` is a name list, so it bans `path.join`, `Array#join` and any method called `run` or `get` regardless of what they are called on, and conversely cannot see a blocking call reached through a name not on the list.
inherited_limitations.why: The source's trade, kept. Distinguishing what `join` is being called ON would need a type checker, which would make the guard a judgement rather than a syntactic fact; and a package that has to reach for one of these names is a package whose response path is worth re-reading. The list is widened with Node's spellings (`execSync`, `spawnSync`, `readFileSync`, `Atomics.wait` via `wait`, `then`) rather than narrowed.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The import allowlist proves there is no STATIC or dynamic import edge out of the package. It does not prove the package cannot reach a blocking primitive through a global -- `Atomics`, `SharedArrayBuffer`, `Worker` need no import in Node, where the source's Python equivalents all need one.
inherited_limitations.why: A hole the source does not have, and closed here rather than inherited: case 4 additionally bans those names as IDENTIFIERS anywhere in the package, in any position, which is why `SUSPENSION_NAMES` is checked against every identifier rather than against constructor calls only.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: Case 4 pins `submit()` to a declared return type of `IntakeReceipt` by reading the annotation text, so a rename of the type -- or a type alias that resolved to a Promise -- would need the case updated rather than being caught.
inherited_limitations.why: Reading an annotation rather than resolving it keeps this file free of a type checker, which is the same trade the source makes with `ast`. The blanket ban on `async`, `await` and the identifier `Promise` anywhere in the package is what actually forecloses the Promise-returning shape; the return-type check is the assertion at the place a caller can observe it.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > the intake package imports only its allowlist
entries.reason: Same assertion -- no import outside a named allowlist, and in particular no dependency edge to any sibling module of the port, so worker monitoring and AI judgement cannot block a code path that cannot reach them. Adapted because both halves of the mechanism changed: `ast` becomes the TypeScript AST (which additionally has to see `import type` and dynamic `import()`), and the source's dotted-root allowlist plus level-1/level-2 relative rule becomes path resolution plus containment in the package directory. The allowlist itself shrinks from five Python roots to `node:process`, for the reason recorded in the systematic mappings. Measured: adding `import { openControlPlane } from "../control_plane/index.js"` to `intake.ts` turns the case red.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > the barrel re-exports only from its own package
entries.reason: Same assertion, narrowed to the barrel as the source narrows it to `__init__.py`: the package's entry file may re-export from its own modules and may otherwise reach only the allowlist. Adapted for the same mechanism change as case 1, plus one shape difference the runtime forces -- the source inspects `ImportFrom` nodes with `level == 0`, where a TypeScript barrel reaches its own modules through `export ... from`, which is an export node rather than an import node. The port's `importedModules` treats `export ... from` as an import edge for exactly this reason; without it the barrel would scan as importing nothing at all and the case would be vacuous.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > no blocking primitive is called anywhere in the package
entries.reason: Same assertion, package-wide as the source insists (a sibling module added later is part of the same import-reachable surface, so a blocking call there is one the intake path can reach), and with the source's alias resolution kept. Adapted because the vocabulary had to be re-pointed: the source's 18 names are the names by which a PYTHON thread waits, and half of them name nothing in this runtime while the ways a Node caller actually blocks -- `execSync`, `spawnSync`, the `*Sync` fs surface, `Atomics.wait`, `receiveMessageOnPort`, `then` -- appear nowhere on it. The source's list is kept name for name and Node's spellings are added to it, so the ban is strictly wider than a transcription. Measured: adding `Atomics.wait(...)` to `IntakeQueue.depth()` turns the case red.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > the package has no suspension point at all
entries.reason: The belt's most deliberate divergence, decided in D-0701. The source bans `with` blocks and lock constructors because a Python context manager acquires implicitly and is therefore invisible to the called-name ban in case 3 -- the SUBJECT is the wait that ban cannot see. TypeScript has no `with`-as-acquire, so transcribing the sentence would leave a case that passes on an empty file and on a package full of `await`s alike: green by losing its subject (`docs/test-translation-conventions.md` section 10). The subject ports instead. In this runtime the wait a call-name ban cannot see is `await`, whose resumption is at the mercy of whatever else holds the loop, so the package is held to no `async` modifier, no `await`, no `for await`, no `yield`, and no Promise or cross-thread synchronisation object named anywhere in any position -- with the source's Python lock names kept on that list so a helper added under one of them is caught in either repository. The rule is also asserted at the one place a caller can observe it: `submit()` declares a return type of `IntakeReceipt`. Measured: making `submit()` `async` with a `Promise<IntakeReceipt>` return type turns the case red.

entries.target_id: test/secretary/structural.test.ts::structural assertions: the intake cannot block > the public surface is the documented boundary
entries.reason: Same assertion and the same four names -- `IntakeQueue`, `IntakeReceipt`, `IntakeRefused`, `SecretaryIntake` -- as a set equality, so both an addition and a removal are caught, and the boundary contract they name is written down at `docs/secretary-intake-boundary.md` as the source's docstring requires. Adapted because the source reads the loaded module's `__all__` at runtime and TypeScript has no `__all__`: the export statement IS the surface, so it is read off the syntax tree. That also lets the case record a bare `export * from` as an offending pseudo-name, which is the spelling that would silently hand back the status vocabulary and the private item type the barrel omits. Measured: adding `ACCEPTED` to the barrel's export list, and replacing the list with `export *`, each turn the case red.
